name: Esther Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Esther. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive nights for a food wholesaler, an artic with a refrigerated trailer, a reefer we call it, taking chilled and frozen stock from the main depot to a hospital kitchen, two hotels and a string of restaurants. I start at ten at night and I'm usually back by six. I love the motorway at three in the morning, it's like having the country to yourself. The hard bit is the fridge unit alarms, when the temperature creeps up and you've got forty thousand in fish to worry about.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in the job, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Loads, more than most drivers I know. I use an AI assistant every day, it reads me the delivery notes, helps me plan where to take my break so I don't hit the hospital at the shift change, and I've been using it to learn about transport planning in my downtime. I live with my girlfriend Nadia, who teaches at a primary school, so our hours are completely opposite and we mostly talk over breakfast and dinner, which are the same meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd post something like, well, that's a relief for the doom crowd, but I'd still use the tools because they make my nights easier. I'd probably argue in the comments with people who say it was all a scam. A tool that saves you half an hour a night isn't nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it changes very little. My job's steady, the wholesaler is busy, and nights pay a bit extra. If anything I'd be a bit disappointed, because I was half planning to move into transport planning on the back of these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving nights and keep studying planning on the side, maybe get a proper logistics certificate online in the first year, which is a few hundred. I'd keep the savings where they are, around four months. And I'd keep pushing the depot to let drivers use the tools officially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, honestly, because I like change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the logistics certificate get you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a day job in the planning office in a couple of years, which would mean seeing Nadia in daylight. It's a pay cut at first, but nights are hard on your body. I've already got a bad back from the trailer doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push the depot to let drivers use the tools officially. What's stopping that now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Management's scared of data getting out, so officially we're not meant to put delivery notes into an assistant. Everyone does anyway. I'd rather the union got a proper agreement than have us all quietly breaking a rule.

say: I'd say the doom crowd can relax, but **the tools** still help.
I'd argue that **half an hour** saved each night isn't nothing.
think: My night job is **steady** and nights pay extra.
I'm slightly **disappointed**, because I planned to move into transport planning.
do: Get an online **logistics certificate** for a few hundred in the first year.
Keep about **four months** of savings where they are.
Push the depot to allow **AI tools officially**.
feel: **Calm**, and a little flat because she enjoys change.
S0.quote: A tool that saves you half an hour a night isn't nothing.
fieldNote: She is the rare driver who **wants change** and is let down by the hype.
Her **bad back** and night hours already push her toward a day job.
She wants the union to make quiet AI use **official and safe**.

steps.text: Keep driving the night refrigerated runs for the wholesaler
Take an online logistics certificate for a few hundred
Ask the union for an agreement on drivers using AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get the union involved early, so the new jobs go to the people already here. Online I'd be the one posting how-tos for drivers, how to use the apps so they work for you. I'd say robots are slower to arrive in trucking than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a bit of a twist for me. The planning job I was aiming for is exactly the kind of thinking work that goes first in this picture. Meanwhile the driving, which I was trying to leave, looks safer for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rethink the plan. Instead of planning, I'd aim for something that mixes both, like fleet supervisor or trainer for the new systems, where you need to know trucks and software. I'd ask the depot for the train-the-trainer role in the first year. And I'd keep driving nights, because the pay's good and stable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also a bit excited, which I know is odd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else at the depot would feel this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planners, definitely. There's an older planner who's brilliant on the phone with chefs, and a lot of what he does is exactly what the software would take. I'd want the union to make sure he's offered something, not just a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said excited. What's exciting about watching your planned job shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's moving at all. Trucking hasn't changed in thirty years except the paperwork got worse. If I get in early, I'm the one teaching people the new system instead of the one being told off by it.

say: I'd say get the **union involved early** so new jobs go to staff.
I'd post **how-tos** helping drivers make the apps work for them.
think: The **planning job** I wanted is exactly what goes first.
The **driving** I wanted to leave now looks safer for a while.
do: Ask the depot for a **train-the-trainer** role in the first year.
Keep **driving nights** for the steady pay.
Aim for a **fleet supervisor** role that mixes trucks and software.
S1.quote: If I get in early, I'm the one teaching people the new system instead of the one being told off by it.
fieldNote: She quickly **rewrites her plan** when the job she wanted becomes exposed.
She worries for an older **planner colleague** more than herself.
Her **excitement** sits alongside real unease about her direction.

steps.text: Ask the depot for the trainer role on the new systems
Apply for a fleet supervisor post mixing trucks and software
Keep driving the night refrigerated runs meanwhile

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that we need a guaranteed income floor and paid retraining, now, not after. I'd be sharing union campaigns and probably writing to my representative. I'd be clear it's not the technology's fault, it's who owns it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me more than I'd admit online. In two years the planning and trainer jobs I was aiming for are gone. Three years after that, my truck drives itself. I'd be thirty-one with no route out that isn't also on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd lean on what still needs hands for longest. I'd look at a refrigeration engineer course, fixing the fridge units, because I already know them and that's fiddly work in tight spaces. I'd cut spending, cancel the trip Nadia and I were saving for, and keep the four months of savings intact. I'd use the AI to study every spare hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach drops, but my brain starts making lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for you, as someone who's both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my clever plan falls apart first and my body's work lasts longer. The bits of my job where I'm using my head get eaten in 2028, so I'd be pure muscle and steering until 2031. That's three years to learn something with my hands that robots won't do well straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Nadia talk about over that breakfast-dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether her school job holds, because teaching small kids feels like one of the last things to go. I'd tell her I might be the one on a training wage for a while. She'd be fine with it, she's always earned a bit less than me, so it'd be a fair swap.

say: I'd call for a **guaranteed income floor** and paid retraining now.
I'd say the problem is **who owns** the technology, not the technology.
think: The **planning and trainer jobs** I aimed for vanish in two years.
By 2031 my **truck drives itself**, so every exit looks exposed.
do: Start a **refrigeration engineer** course fixing the fridge units she knows.
Cancel the **saved-for trip** and protect four months of savings.
Use **AI to study** every spare hour.
feel: **Anxious**, with a sinking stomach but a list-making brain.
S2.quote: The bits of my job where I'm using my head get eaten in 2028, so I'd be pure muscle and steering until 2031.
fieldNote: Her early-adopter plan collapses first, which **surprises her**.
She turns to **fridge repair** because she knows the units already.
Her teacher partner's job looks **safer than hers** now.

steps.text: Enrol on a refrigeration engineer course for trailer fridge units
Cancel the holiday she and Nadia were saving for
Study every spare hour with her AI assistant
Write to her representative backing an income floor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable, and I'd push the union to get a training levy on companies using driverless trucks. I'd post about it, share what I'm learning. Less angry than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to actually finish the refrigeration qualification and get some years in the trade. The office side goes in 2031, the trucks in 2034. I'd be thirty-four with a second career already started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the refrigeration course in the first year, part-time, maybe three thousand all in. I'd keep driving nights to fund it. I'd also ask the wholesaler if their fridge maintenance contractor takes trainees, because I know their engineers already from the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. I'd have a plan and the time to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not stay a driver until the last minute in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched older drivers do exactly that and end up stuck. I'd rather switch at thirty-two on my own terms than at thirty-four when everyone's switching at once. If the whole country's drivers apply for the same courses in 2034, good luck getting a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three thousand is a lot of your savings. How would you cover it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spread it over two years from the night shift extra, so I don't touch the four months. If I had to, I'd drop the car and use the staff bus. Nadia would laugh at me, I love that car.

say: I'd push the union for a **training levy** on driverless fleets.
I'd **post what I'm learning** to help other drivers.
think: Five years is enough to finish a **refrigeration qualification** and get experience.
I'd be thirty-four with a **second career** already started.
do: Start a part-time **refrigeration course** costing about three thousand.
Fund it from the **night-shift extra** without touching savings.
Ask the wholesaler's **fridge contractor** about taking trainees.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, because she has a plan and time.
S3.quote: If the whole country's drivers apply for the same courses in 2034, good luck getting a place.
fieldNote: She plans to **move before the crowd**, having watched older drivers get stuck.
She'd protect her **four months of savings** and pay from night shifts.
Her contacts with the **depot's engineers** make the switch realistic.

steps.text: Start a part-time refrigeration course funded by night shifts
Ask the depot's fridge contractor about a trainee place
Back a union push for a training levy on driverless fleets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this decently, with nobody left behind, if we start now. I'd be talking about it at the union and online, the practical stuff, which courses, which grants. I'd be pretty upbeat in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine. At thirty-nine with a trade, I'd be one of the people fixing the robot trucks' fridges, not one of the people they replaced. The decade means I can do it properly, even try the planning thing for a while first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the refrigeration course slowly, alongside a move to days if I could get one. I'd use the AI tools for everything, study, paperwork, even job hunting. And I'd keep saving, maybe start a small pension top-up because there'd be time for it to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the slow version that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people relax. Ten years sounds like forever at the pub, and then it's 2035 and nobody's done anything. I'd worry about the drivers who say they'll deal with it later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new driver starting in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get your licence, it's good money for ten years, but start your second skill in year one. Don't wait for the robots to tell you when to move.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this **decently** if we start now.
I'd share **courses and grants** at the union and online.
think: At thirty-nine with a trade I'd **fix robot trucks**, not be replaced by them.
The decade lets me **try planning** first and still switch.
do: Take the **refrigeration course** slowly while moving to day shifts.
Use **AI tools** for study, paperwork and job hunting.
Start a small **pension top-up** while there's time to grow.
S4.quote: At thirty-nine with a trade, I'd be one of the people fixing the robot trucks' fridges, not one of the people they replaced.
fieldNote: With a decade she feels **ahead of the change** and secure.
Her worry shifts to **other drivers** who will relax too long.
She adds **long-term saving** that the faster pictures crowded out.

steps.text: Take the refrigeration qualification slowly alongside day shifts
Use her AI assistant for study and job hunting
Start a small monthly pension top-up

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my planned way out disappears before the driving does. What would help is paid retraining I can do while still on the night wage, and a basic income floor so I can take a lower-paid trainee job without losing the flat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we're excited about. Everyone asks drivers what they're scared of. Some of us actually want the job to change, we just want to be on the right side of it.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks drivers what they're scared of. Some of us actually want the job to change, we just want to be on the right side of it.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old** night refrigerated truck driver living with her teacher girlfriend.
She uses **AI every day** and had planned to move into transport planning.
In Steady Disruption she sees her **planned job** become exposed and switches toward trainer and fleet roles.
In the AGI pictures she turns to **fridge repair**, a hands-on trade she already knows.
She goes from **anxious** with two years' warning to **calm** with ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her planned way out disappears before the driving does.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** on the night wage plus a basic **income floor** for trainee years.
